content:
Epic Games has submitted a response to Apple's earlier application for the court to order both parties to attend settlement talks. Details are as follows.

Epic believes that court-ordered settlement talks would not be beneficial

Last Thursday, Apple submitted a proposed commission structure regarding in-app purchases completed outside the App Store system within the United States.

Under Apple's proposed plan, the company would charge a commission of up to 15% on transactions completed through alternative payment systems.

On the same day, Apple filed another motion requesting Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

In its motion, Apple stated that "discussing potential settlement solutions in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the chances of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding a lengthy remand proceeding."

Epic has now responded to Apple's motion, stating that although the company "has always been, and remains, willing to consider any serious settlement proposal proactively put forward by Apple to introduce competition and benefit all developers," it "does not believe that referring the matter to a settlement conference at this stage would effectively increase the chances of reaching a settlement."

Epic added in its response that "if the court orders the case to be referred to a settlement conference, Epic will participate in good faith."

It is now up to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to decide whether to refer the case to a settlement conference. Apple has requested that the conference be conducted under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.

9to5Mac commentary

Apple has repeatedly attempted to narrow the scope of the injunction issued by Judge Gonzalez Rogers regarding purchases outside the App Store. Apple has specifically argued that, since Epic's lawsuit is not a class action, the injunction should not broadly apply to other developers.

For example, Apple argued in one of its appeals that developers seeking similar relief should file their own lawsuits rather than benefit from the injunction in Epic's case. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Apple's attempt to narrow the injunction, ruling that limiting the injunction to Epic and its affiliates would not provide Epic with the complete relief it sought.

The reasoning behind this ruling is also consistent with Epic's public stance throughout most of the case—its fight goes beyond its own commercial interests and aims to benefit a broader range of developers.

In its motion requesting that the case be referred to (confidential) settlement talks, Apple did not indicate what proposal it might put forward. However, anyone closely following the case would likely agree that Apple would probably seek a deal particularly favourable to Epic, while limiting any concessions to Epic itself.

In fact, Epic's response has pre-empted such thinking, stating that Apple's "serious settlement proposal" must "benefit all developers," and hinting at the end of its response that Apple's efforts may be too late.

If you were Apple, what proposal would you put forward to Epic Games? Feel free to share with us in the comments section.
